clue.text: Can't do something for this sucker? How useless!

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom 'can't do it for love nor this', said of a hopeless performer
second meaning: a sweet that is sucked rather than chewed

explanation.surface: Someone sighs over a hopeless dupe who cannot manage a simple task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't do it for toffee' is British slang for being hopeless at something; 'sucker' looks like a gullible person but is a sweet you suck. 'How useless!' rounds off the first sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee is a chewy boiled sweet, often sucked slowly, and appears in the British idiom meaning utterly incapable.

clue.text: Nymph lacks opening for increased publicity

indicators.note: lacking an opening means the phrase that follows loses its very first letter

blocks.note: increased means more
an ad is a piece of publicity

explanation.surface: A shy nymph misses her chance at greater fame.
explanation.definitionFit: An oread is a mountain nymph in Greek mythology, one particular kind of nature spirit.

clue.text: Excellent worker in firm — one co-opted originally

indicators.note: in places the worker inside the word for a firm
originally points to the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: firm, as in held fast
the worker ant is a crossword staple
Roman numeral one
first letter of co-opted

explanation.surface: A company praises a fine employee who was brought in from outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The worker sits in F_AST, then I and C follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantastic is informal praise meaning extremely good, a direct synonym of excellent.

clue.text: Frightful rage about Women's Institute pest

indicators.note: frightful suggests something dreadfully messed up, so the letters are thrown into disorder
about means surrounding, so the shuffled word wraps round the institute

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
WI is the abbreviation for the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation

explanation.surface: A furious outburst about the Women's Institute, treated as a nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: The earwig is a garden insect that damages plants, a familiar example of a pest.

clue.text: It is easy to follow the rag hero in church books

indicators.note: to rag is to tease or play pranks, so the word next to it gets knocked about
in puts the reworked word inside the church abbreviation

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
taken as written, to be rearranged
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A student newspaper's hero appears in parish records.
explanation.walkthrough: A rag is also a student magazine, which is the sense the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: A coherent argument holds together logically, so a reader can track it without trouble.

clue.text: Disparage one's wares in a heat wave?

definitions.note: a whimsical second sense: what a fishmonger might have to do in hot weather

blocks.note: first meaning: the old idiom for running down your own goods or efforts
second meaning, read literally: a hot spell spoils fish, and the seller has to say so

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal reading: in hot weather unsold fish goes off.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a trader belittling their own merchandise, from a fishmonger admitting the catch had gone bad.

clue.text: A breather for me

blocks.note: surface reading: a short rest, the interval in a match
setter's reading: the two letters of me make up exactly one half of the four-letter word for a period of hours

explanation.walkthrough: 'me' is the second half of the word TIME, so the answer also describes the clue's last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The interval in a football or rugby match gives players a short rest between the two periods of play.

clue.text: Material always taken in and not put up outside

indicators.note: taken in means held inside, so always sits within the other word
in a down clue, putting a word up writes it from bottom to top

blocks.note: ay, or aye, is an old word for always
nor means and not

explanation.surface: Fabric that is always taken in at the seams but never hung up outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is a synthetic textile made from cellulose, so it is a kind of material.

clue.text: A new food caught off the Massachusetts coast?

definitions.note: a place found there, not a phrase of the same part of speech

blocks.note: surface reading: fishermen landing some novel seafood out at sea
setter's reading: the place itself, an island off New England whose name seems to break into words for bread and for food

explanation.surface: Fishermen land some strange new edible catch out in the waters off New England.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a pun on the name: naan is an Indian bread and tuck is British school slang for food, so the island seems to have food in its name. No full letter-by-letter wordplay accounts for every word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantucket is an island lying about thirty miles south of Cape Cod, in the Atlantic just off the Massachusetts mainland.

clue.text: Plant for a girl like Marie Antoinette

blocks.note: Penny is a girl's name
Marie Antoinette was a queen, so royal

explanation.surface: A garden plant chosen for a girl who resembles the French queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennyroyal is a species of mint, a small aromatic herb, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Tug operator, perhaps, in Boston?

definitions.note: an example: a worker in Boston is an American

blocks.note: first meaning: a sharp pull
second meaning: someone working in a New England city is an American, a Northerner in particular

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tugboat skipper in Boston harbour; the two halves are a verb for pulling and a slang word for an American.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden pull is a yank, and Yank is informal for an American, originally a New Englander.

clue.text: Utopian catalogue of archetypes

blocks.note: in Plato an idea is an archetype or perfect form
a catalogue is a list

explanation.surface: A dreamer's inventory of perfect models.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads the pieces in reverse: a list of ideas, with the archetype coming first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Utopian dreams of a perfect society, just as an idealist pursues lofty principles over practical concerns.

clue.text: Language, often held to be quiet

definitions.note: idiom: you hold it to keep silent

blocks.note: first meaning: a language
second meaning: the body part people hold when told to keep silent

explanation.definitionFit: Tongue is an old word for a spoken language, and the mouth organ you hold to stop speaking.

clue.text: Way to circumvent business levy in the past

indicators.note: to circumvent is to go around something, so the road abbreviation wraps the other piece

blocks.note: St is street, a way
Co is company

explanation.surface: A route for dodging an old tax on trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Scot was a medieval tax or levy, surviving in the phrase scot-free for escaping payment.

clue.text: One concerned about imprisoned craftsman

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the person concerned goes round the other word

blocks.note: a carer is one who is concerned for others
pent, as in pent up, means shut in

explanation.surface: Someone worrying about a tradesman who has been locked up.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter is a skilled tradesman working with wood, so a craftsman.

clue.text: Specify a Japanese liquor, nominally a double

blocks.note: to name is to specify
sake is Japanese rice wine

explanation.surface: Ordering a Japanese drink, then a double measure of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' suggests a bar order; here it means a twin in title only.
explanation.definitionFit: A namesake shares a person's name, so they are a double by name alone.

clue.text: Grim situation on board

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer: something found on a ship

blocks.note: stern means grim
a post is a position or job

explanation.surface: A dreadful predicament aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is a loose definition: the answer is a part of a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The sternpost is the main upright timber at the rear of a ship's hull, found aboard any wooden vessel.

clue.text: High-class officer somehow tops the poll

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive by some unspecified route, so their order is not fixed

blocks.note: U means upper class
taken as written

explanation.surface: A high-ranking officer somehow wins the election.
explanation.walkthrough: Poll is an old word for the head, so the definition means sits on top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A coiffure is an arranged hairstyle, which sits on top of the head, the poll.

clue.text: Brother caught with gripes, mostly from vegetables

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the word for gripes loses its final letter

blocks.note: short for brother
c for caught in cricket scoring
colic is a griping stomach pain

explanation.surface: A sibling got stomach pains from eating his greens.
explanation.definitionFit: Broccoli is a green vegetable; the word is plural in Italian, matching the clue's plural.

clue.text: Artist to whom little Elizabeth lost her head

indicators.note: losing a head means the first letter of the name falls away

blocks.note: Betty is a pet form of Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A painter for whom a young girl fell dizzily in love.
explanation.definitionFit: William Etty was a 19th-century English painter known for nudes, so an artist.

clue.text: Entering study, ring up for a voucher

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the ring and up pieces go into the study word

blocks.note: to con is to study
O is ring-shaped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Coming into an office, someone telephones to ask for a voucher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring up' looks like making a phone call; the ring is O and up is taken as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupon is a slip giving a discount or entitlement, which is what a voucher does.

clue.text: Misrepresent the origin of Freudian doctrine

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

blocks.note: to belie is to give a false idea of
first letter of Freudian

explanation.surface: Distorting where Freud's theories came from.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctrine is a principle held to be true, which is a belief.

clue.text: Characteristic expression of primitive instincts upheld by Man

blocks.note: the id in Freudian theory is the seat of primitive instincts
IOM is the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A phrase revealing basic urges, supported by humanity.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer one piece is held up by the piece below it, so 'upheld by' just places Man after the instincts. Man here is the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a phrase or turn of speech peculiar to a language or person, a characteristic expression.

clue.text: Trouble involving one's dogs? Well, well!

indicators.note: trouble means disturb, so the letters it governs are stirred up

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at the trouble their dogs have caused.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodness, like well, well, is a mild exclamation of surprise.

clue.text: As did this creature from-- proclaimed in 5 dn?

definitions.note: past tense: what the fish in 5 down did

blocks.note: first meaning: a small silvery food fish

blocks.clueFragment: As did this creature from-- proclaimed in 5 dn
blocks.note: second meaning: the past tense of the verb that 5 down says a stale fish does

explanation.walkthrough: 5 down calls the fish stinking, so it gave off an odour; the fish named is also the past tense of smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A smelt is a small edible sea fish, and smelt is the British past tense of smell.

clue.text: Free tuition — that's partly the case

indicators.note: partly says only a portion of the phrase is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Free teaching is only partly the true state of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the case' reads as 'what is true'; it is an object.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles or cosmetics, a crossword favourite.

clue.text: Rascally peacekeeper gadded about, as bad as ever

blocks.note: the UN keeps peace
an imp is a rascal
roved means wandered about

explanation.surface: A mischievous soldier went gallivanting and is no better behaved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rascally' is an adjective standing for the rascal; it attaches loosely to IMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unimproved has not got any better, so it remains as bad as it always was.

clue.text: Burial-place of Conservative student in Italian city church

indicators.note: in places the student inside the name of the city

blocks.note: C for Conservative
Rome is the Italian capital
L for learner
CH for church

explanation.surface: The grave of a Tory student lies in a church in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the learner plate on a British learner driver's car, hence student.
explanation.definitionFit: A cromlech is a prehistoric stone tomb, a megalithic burial chamber, so a burial-place.

clue.text: Jot down signs of lack of accommodation for art

blocks.note: no means none
the Tate is a London art gallery

explanation.surface: Taking notes on symptoms of a housing shortage for artists.
explanation.definitionFit: To notate is to write in notation, setting down musical or other symbols.
